title: The Difference a Form Makes: Gerunds, Infinitives and Meaning
paragraphs: English grammar students often learn gerunds and infinitives as two parallel systems: some verbs take one, some take the other, and the challenge is simply to memorise which is which. This is not wrong, but it is incomplete. The more interesting story is that many of the most common verbs in English take both forms — but with a change in meaning that is subtle, significant, and often misunderstood.

"I stopped to smoke" and "I stopped smoking" describe two completely different situations. In the first, I stopped what I was doing in order to smoke — smoking was the purpose of the stopping. In the second, I stopped the habit of smoking — the smoking itself came to an end. The infinitive after "stop" expresses purpose; the gerund expresses the activity that has ended. This is not a superficial grammatical rule: it reflects something real about how the mind organises time and intention.

"I remember meeting her" and "I remember to meet her" are similarly distinct. The gerund expresses a memory of a past event — the meeting has already happened. The infinitive expresses a prospective obligation — I remember that I need to meet her. The same applies to "forget": "I forgot meeting him" means I have no memory of that past event; "I forgot to meet him" means I failed to do something I was supposed to do.

"She tried drinking the coffee" (gerund) and "She tried to drink the coffee" (infinitive) also differ. With the gerund, she experimented with drinking it — she attempted it as a test or trial. With the infinitive, she made an effort to drink it but possibly failed. "Try + gerund" suggests experiment; "try + infinitive" suggests effort toward a goal that may not be achieved.

"Going on" has its own system. "She went on talking for an hour" (gerund) means she continued talking — the activity persisted. "She went on to become a professor" (infinitive) means she moved on to a new stage in her life. These are almost opposite meanings: continuation versus progression.

"Regret" follows a similar logic. "I regret telling her" (gerund) means I am sorry that I told her — I told her and now feel remorse about it. "I regret to tell you" (infinitive) is a formal phrase meaning "I am sorry to inform you" — the regret is about the information that follows, and the telling has not yet happened. The gerund looks backward; the infinitive looks forward.

Understanding these distinctions is not merely a grammatical exercise. It is an exercise in temporal and intentional precision. The English speaker who can distinguish "I remember doing it" from "I remember to do it" has a linguistic tool for expressing the relationship between memory, obligation, and time with a precision that many languages handle differently or more clumsily. At B1 level, using these distinctions accurately is one of the clearest markers of advanced English proficiency.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: I have such a bad memory. I completely forgot meeting Professor Akhmetov at the conference last year.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Or did you forget to meet him? Those are different things.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: "Forgot meeting him" — you met him but have no memory of it. "Forgot to meet him" — you were supposed to meet him but didn't show up.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Oh — it was the first one. I met him but genuinely have no memory of the conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: That's either a very bad memory or a very boring conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: He's actually fascinating. Which makes it worse. I must have been exhausted. I remember being at the conference — just not that particular moment.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: And now you remember meeting him? Because knowing about it makes it feel more real.

keyPhrases.context: "A prospective obligation." = something you still need to do in the future.
"I told her and now feel remorse." = a deep feeling of guilt about a past action.
"Temporal and intentional precision." = precise about time and intention.
"The activity persisted." = it continued; it didn't stop.
"Try + gerund suggests experiment." = testing something to see the result.
"Advanced English proficiency." = a high level of ability in the language.
"Continuation versus progression." = moving to the next stage.
"Handle differently or more clumsily." = in a less precise or awkward way.

vocab.definition: deep regret for a wrong done
vocab.example: "I regret telling her" = I told her and now feel remorse.

vocab.definition: expected or likely in the future
vocab.example: "Remember to do" = a prospective obligation. Still needs to happen.

vocab.definition: to continue doing something despite difficulty; to remain
vocab.example: "She went on talking" — the activity persisted. Continued without stopping.
"Temporal and intentional precision." — exact about time and intention.

vocab.definition: a high level of ability or skill
vocab.example: "Advanced English proficiency." — ability to use English at a high level.
"Temporal precision" = being exact about when something happened or will happen.

vocab.definition: a plan or aim; what you intend to do
vocab.example: "The mind organises time and intention." — what you planned to do.

vocab.definition: existing only at the surface; not thorough or deep
vocab.example: "This is not a superficial grammatical rule." — not just a surface-level rule.

task1Items.question: "I stopped to smoke" — the infinitive expresses ___ (why I stopped).
"I stopped smoking" — the gerund means the habit ___ .
"I remember meeting her" (gerund) — the meeting is a ___ event.
"I remember to meet her" (infinitive) — the meeting is a ___ obligation.
"She tried drinking coffee" (gerund) = she ___ with it as a test.
"She tried to drink coffee" (infinitive) = she made an ___ toward a goal.
"I regret telling her" (gerund) — the gerund looks ___ into the past.

task2Items.statement: "I stopped to smoke" and "I stopped smoking" mean the same thing.
After "remember," gerund = past event; infinitive = future obligation.
"Try + gerund" suggests effort toward a goal.
"Try + infinitive" suggests effort toward a goal that may not be achieved.
"She went on to become a professor" means she continued to be a professor.
"I regret to tell you" is a formal phrase about information that follows.
Rustam forgot to meet the professor (he had an appointment but didn't show up).
The text says this distinction is an exercise in temporal and intentional precision.

questions.text: What does "I stopped to smoke" mean?
opts: I stopped the habit of smoking
I stopped what I was doing in order to smoke
questions.correct: I stopped what I was doing in order to smoke
questions.hint: "Stopped to smoke" = stopped [other activity] in order to smoke (purpose). ✅

questions.text: What does "I remember meeting her" mean?
opts: I need to meet her soon
I don't want to meet her
I have a memory of a past meeting
questions.correct: I have a memory of a past meeting
questions.hint: "Remember + gerund" = memory of a past event. The meeting already happened. ✅

questions.text: What does "She tried drinking the coffee" (gerund) suggest?
opts: She made an effort but failed
She tested it as an experiment
questions.correct: She tested it as an experiment
questions.hint: "Try + gerund" = experiment/test — she tried it to see what would happen. ✅

questions.text: What is the difference between "went on talking" and "went on to become"?
opts: "Went on talking" = continued; "went on to become" = moved to a new stage
questions.correct: "Went on talking" = continued; "went on to become" = moved to a new stage
questions.hint: "Go on + gerund" = continue. "Go on + infinitive" = progress to a new thing. ✅

questions.text: "I regret ___ her" = I told her and now feel sorry. (gerund or infinitive?)
questions.hint: "I regret TELLING her" = gerund. I told her (past) and now feel remorse. ✅

questions.text: Which verb+form combination looks "backward" at the past?
questions.hint: "Regret + gerund" = looking backward. I regret what I did in the past. ✅

questions.text: "I told her and now feel remorse." "Remorse" means:
opts: Deep regret about a past action
questions.correct: Deep regret about a past action
questions.hint: "remorse" = deep guilt and regret about something you did that was wrong or harmful.

opts: Expected or likely in the future
questions.correct: Expected or likely in the future
questions.hint: "prospective" = relating to the future; expected to happen.

opts: I met him but have no memory of it
I was supposed to meet him but didn't
questions.correct: I met him but have no memory of it
questions.hint: "Forgot + gerund (meeting)" = the meeting happened; I have no memory of it. ✅

questions.text: "I forgot to meet him." — What happened?
opts: I have no memory of meeting him
I was supposed to meet him but failed to do so
I don't want to meet him
questions.correct: I was supposed to meet him but failed to do so
questions.hint: "Forgot + to-infinitive (to meet)" = I was supposed to meet him (future obligation) but didn't. ✅
